extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, psychology, and social science interested in the methodology and foundations of a science of human nature
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological standards for regarding the study of mental phenomena as a science (what counts as laws of mind, how mental phenomena should be studied, and what predictive or explanatory claims are appropriate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject qualifies as a science
rubrics_metrics.description: Any facts are fitted, in themselves, to be a subject of science which follow one another according to constant laws, although those laws may not have been discovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: meteorology and tidology both depend on laws even if those laws are not fully known; a discipline is a science if its phenomena depend on discoverable laws, even when practical prediction is difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exactness depends on accounting for all causes
rubrics_metrics.description: A science is exact only when its laws comprehend the whole of the causes which influence the phenomena, whether in a great or trifling degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast astronomy (which became exact when perturbations were accounted for) with tidology (not exact because many minor causes are not fully ascertained). Exactness is a matter of scope of causal knowledge and measurability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate generalizations acceptable for social/political purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximate generalizations that are almost always true for large classes may be equivalent to universal propositions for political and social science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many human phenomena depend chiefly on general causes common to large groups, propositions true 'in the main' are sufficient for governing expectations and conduct in social contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science of human nature must connect generalizations to underlying laws
rubrics_metrics.description: To have genuine scientific character, approximate generalizations must be connected deductively with the laws of nature from which they result, showing their proper limits and enabling deduction in new circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The value of social generalizations increases when they can be exhibited as corollaries of universal laws, permitting extension and delimitation beyond mere empirical regularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive scope: individuals vs masses
rubrics_metrics.description: Precise prediction of an individual’s thoughts, feelings, or actions is not possible because data are never complete; yet predictions about masses or large classes can be made reliably when general causes dominate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit expectations about predictive power: use probabilistic/approximate predictions for individuals, and treat aggregate predictions as the proper domain for political and social applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'laws of mind'
rubrics_metrics.description: By the laws of mind are meant the laws according to which mental phenomena (thoughts, emotions, volitions, sensations) generate one another — the regularities of succession among mental states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sensations as mental states even though their immediate antecedents are bodily; concentrate on the succession relations among mental phenomena themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish laws of mind from laws of body
rubrics_metrics.description: All states of mind are immediately caused either by other states of mind (laws of Mind) or by states of body (laws of Body/physiology); the distinction matters for classification and method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if physiological antecedents exist for mental states, the characteristics of those nervous states are unknown; therefore mental science should study mental successions directly rather than purely infer them from physiology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and ascertainability of uniformities among mental states
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist uniformities of succession among states of mind, and these can be ascertained by observation and experiment; this supports a distinct science of mind (psychology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if mental laws are derivative of physiological laws, they must be studied on their own terms because physiological details are currently inaccessible or unknowable in sufficient detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of association (three principal laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: First: an excited state of consciousness can later be reproduced as an inferior degree (every impression has its idea). Second: similar ideas tend to excite one another. Third: greater intensity in impressions is equivalent to greater frequency of conjunction in producing association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elementary laws (drawn from Hume and James Mill) are foundations for building more complex psychological laws by experimental inquiry and observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental chemistry / generation of complex ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex mental phenomena may be generated by the blending or coalescence of many simpler ideas, sometimes producing a new simple-appearing state (analogy to chemical combination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where elements coalesce into apparently simple feelings, it is proper to say the complex idea 'results from' simpler ones, not necessarily that it 'consists' of them; examples include perception of shape or extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume derivation proves sufficiency — require direct study of complex phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a complex mental phenomenon can in principle be generated from simpler ones, that does not remove the necessity for experimental study of the generated phenomenon itself; knowledge of constituents does not substitute for observation of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: knowing properties of oxygen and sulphur does not enable deduction of sulphuric acid properties without specific experiment; likewise, psychologists must study belief, desire, volition empirically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological requirement for establishing causal claims (Agreement and Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing that one class of mental states causes another requires not merely the Method of Agreement (co-occurrence), but also the Method of Difference (showing change when the candidate cause is absent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove, for example, that a particular association generates moral reprobation, one must (a) show they co-occur generally and (b) test whether introducing that associated idea to a previously indifferent action produces disapproval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate influence of bodily states while privileging psychological analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in mental susceptibility among individuals may arise from original predisposition, prior mental history, or physical organization; physiological influences are important but should not be accepted crudely as the sole basis for empirical generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical differences often work through psychological mediators (e.g., intensity of sensation leading to stronger ideas and desires); analysts should parse whether effects are direct physiological influences or mediated by mental laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for moral freedom and self-formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral freedom is the consciousness that one can modify one's own character if one wishes; complete freedom requires either success in forming character or that one’s wishes would be strong enough in conflict to prevail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess moral freedom by whether a person feels habits/temptations are their masters or theirs to master, and whether they have formed confirmed virtues indicative of exercised self-formation.
